question: A 9-month-old female infant is brought in by her mother to the pediatrician because she is concerned that her daughter is not growing normally. On physical exam, the head circumference is 95th percentile and the height is 5th percentile. The child has disproportionate growth such that both the upper and lower extremities show a rhizomelic pattern of shortening, but the axial skeleton appears to be normal. The child appears to have normal intelligence, but has delayed motor milestones; specifically, she is not able to roll or sit up by herself. Which of the following best describes the mode of inheritance for this disorder?
reasoning_chain: CHAIN: "9-month-old female infant" -> "disproportionate growth" -> "rhizomelic pattern of shortening" -> "normal intelligence" -> "delayed motor milestones" -> "possible genetic disorder" -> "likely autosomal recessive inheritance" -> 85%

CHAIN: "9-month-old female infant" -> "head circumference 95th percentile" -> "height 5th percentile" -> "disproportionate growth" -> "suggestive of skeletal dysplasia" -> "normal intelligence" -> "possible genetic condition" -> "autosomal dominant inheritance less likely" -> 75%

CHAIN: "9-month-old female infant" -> "disproportionate growth" -> "rhizomelic shortening" -> "normal axial skeleton" -> "delayed motor milestones" -> "possible genetic disorder" -> "X-linked inheritance less likely" -> 70%

CHAIN: "9-month-old female infant" -> "disproportionate growth" -> "rhizomelic pattern" -> "normal intelligence" -> "delayed motor milestones" -> "suggestive of a specific genetic condition" -> "mitochondrial inheritance unlikely" -> 60%
analysis: The clinical presentation of disproportionate growth with rhizomelic shortening of the limbs and normal intelligence suggests a skeletal dysplasia, likely achondroplasia, which is known to have an autosomal dominant inheritance pattern. The head circumference being at the 95th percentile and the height at the 5th percentile further supports this diagnosis. Therefore, the mode of inheritance for this disorder is best described as autosomal dominant.
